exercises.prompt: Which of these would let a current flow through them easily? Choose **all** that do.

options.label: A copper wire
options.feedback: Yes. Copper is a metal with many free electrons, which is why almost all wires are made of it.

options.label: A plastic ruler
options.feedback: Not yet. In plastic every electron is held tightly by its atom, so plastic is an insulator.

options.label: A strip of aluminium foil
options.feedback: Yes. Aluminium is a metal and a good conductor; overhead power cables are mostly aluminium.

options.label: A rubber band
options.feedback: Not yet. Rubber is an insulator, which is why it is used for gloves and cable coverings.

options.label: The graphite "lead" of a pencil
options.feedback: Yes, surprisingly. Graphite is a form of carbon with free electrons, so it conducts, though not as well as a metal.

hints: A conductor needs charges that are free to move. Which of these materials are metals?
One non-metal on the list is a conductor too. Pencil "lead" is not lead at all: it is graphite, a form of carbon.
exercises.solution: The conductors are **the copper wire, the aluminium foil and the graphite pencil lead**. Copper and aluminium are metals, whose outer electrons wander freely. Graphite is unusual: it is not a metal, but its carbon atoms are arranged in sheets with electrons that can move along them, so it conducts. Plastic and rubber hold their electrons tightly, so they are insulators.

exercises.prompt: Aiko rubs a balloon on her hair. Afterwards the balloon is negatively charged. What happened?

options.label: Electrons moved from her hair onto the balloon.
options.feedback: Yes. The balloon gained extra electrons, so it is negative; her hair lost some, so it is positive.

options.label: Protons moved from the balloon onto her hair.
options.feedback: Not yet. Protons sit in the heavy nucleus at the centre of each atom and do not move from one object to another when you rub them. It is the light electrons that move.

options.label: Rubbing created new negative charge in the balloon.
options.feedback: Not yet. Charge is never created or destroyed; it can only be moved from place to place.

options.label: The balloon became negative because it got warm.
options.feedback: Not yet. Rubbing does warm things a little, but warmth does not make charge. Something had to move.

hints: Charge can't be made from nothing. So something carrying charge must have moved.
Which particles are light and loosely held on the outside of atoms: protons or electrons?
exercises.solution: Rubbing moved **electrons from Aiko's hair onto the balloon**. Electrons carry negative charge, so the balloon, with extra electrons, is negative, and her hair, with fewer electrons than protons, is positive. No charge was created: the total stayed the same, it was just shared out differently. Each positive hair now repels the others, which is why her hair stands on end.

exercises.prompt: A torch draws a current of **2 A** for **5 minutes**. How many coulombs of charge flow through its bulb? (Remember that 1 A is 1 coulomb per second.)

feedback.message: Close: you multiplied 2 by 5. But the current is in coulombs per **second**, so the time must be in seconds. How many seconds are in 5 minutes?
Not yet. 120 is the number of coulombs in one minute. The torch is on for 5 minutes.

hints: Current is charge per second, so charge = current × time, with the time in seconds.
exercises.solution:
Current tells you how many coulombs pass each second. In 5 minutes there are $5 \times 60 = 300$ seconds, so

$$Q = I \times t = 2\ \text{A} \times 300\ \text{s} = 600\ \text{C}.$$

So **600 coulombs** flow through the bulb, which is about $600 \times 6.24 \times 10^{18} \approx 3.7 \times 10^{21}$ electrons.

exercises.prompt: A **9 V** battery pushes **20 coulombs** of charge round a circuit. How many **joules** of energy does the battery hand to that charge?

feedback.message: Not yet: you added the numbers. One volt means one joule **for every** coulomb, so 9 volts means 9 joules for each of the 20 coulombs.

hints: One volt means one joule for every coulomb of charge.
So a 9 V battery gives 9 joules to each coulomb. How much for 20 coulombs?
exercises.solution:
Voltage is energy per coulomb, so energy = voltage × charge:

$$9\ \text{J per coulomb} \times 20\ \text{coulombs} = 180\ \text{J}.$$

The battery hands **180 joules** to the charge, which delivers it to the bulb, motor or buzzer in the circuit.

exercises.prompt: Wanjiru, in Nairobi, sees a flash of lightning and counts **9 seconds** before she hears the thunder. About how many **kilometres** away was the lightning?

feedback.message: Not yet: you multiplied. Sound takes about 3 seconds to cover each kilometre, so divide the seconds by 3.

hints: Light arrives almost at once. The delay is the time the sound takes to reach you.
Sound covers about one kilometre every 3 seconds.
exercises.solution: Sound travels about 343 metres per second, so it needs roughly 3 seconds per kilometre. The light arrives practically instantly, so the 9-second delay is the sound's journey: $9 \div 3 = 3$. The lightning was about **3 kilometres** away. That is close enough to be dangerous: Wanjiru should already be indoors.

exercises.prompt: Thunder rumbles while Rahul is playing football in a park in Chennai. Where is the safest place for him to go?

options.label: Under the tallest tree in the park, to keep dry
options.feedback: Not yet. A tall tree, especially one on its own, is one of the most likely things to be struck, and lightning can jump from the trunk to someone sheltering beneath it.

options.label: Into the middle of the open field, away from everything
options.feedback: Not yet. In an open field a person is often the tallest thing around. Open ground is dangerous in a storm.

options.label: Inside a proper building, such as a house or a school
options.feedback: Yes. A building with wiring and plumbing gives lightning paths to the ground around you. Stay inside until about half an hour after the last thunder.

options.label: Under the small open roof of a bus stop
options.feedback: Not yet. Small open shelters keep the rain off, but they do not protect you from lightning.

hints: If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck.
Lightning tends to hit tall, isolated things. What kind of shelter surrounds you and gives the current a path round you to the ground?
exercises.solution: The safest choice is **inside a proper building**. Its wiring, plumbing and structure give lightning paths to the ground that go round the people inside. A tree on its own, an open field and a small open shelter all leave you exposed. Rahul should go indoors as soon as he hears thunder, keep away from showers and plugged-in devices during the storm, and wait about half an hour after the last thunder before going back out.

exercises.prompt: In the water analogy, a battery is like a pump and a wire is like a pipe. Which of these statements is **true of water but not of electricity**?

options.label: If you cut it, the stuff flowing inside pours out of the cut end.
options.feedback: Yes. Cut a water pipe and water sprays out; cut a wire and no charge pours out, because air is an insulator. The current simply stops all round the loop.

options.label: The stuff flowing round the loop is not used up.
options.feedback: Not yet. This is true of both: water goes round and round, and so does charge. Only energy is handed over.

options.label: A bigger push from the pump makes more flow.
options.feedback: Not yet. This is true of both: a higher voltage usually drives a larger current, as a stronger pump drives more water.

options.label: Energy is delivered where the flow does work, at a wheel or a bulb.
options.feedback: Not yet. This is true of both, and it is one of the best features of the analogy.

hints: Three of these statements are things the analogy gets right. Look for the one it gets wrong.
Think about what happens at a cut end of a pipe, and at a cut end of a wire.
exercises.solution: Only **(a)** is true of water but not of electricity. Charge can only flow through a conductor, and air is an insulator, so at a cut wire the charge has nowhere to go: the current stops everywhere in the loop at once. The other three statements are what make the analogy useful: the flow is not used up, a bigger push means more flow, and energy is delivered where the flow does work.

exercises.prompt: The unit of electric current is named after a French scientist who, in the 1820s, measured how currents push and pull on each other. What is the unit called?
exercises.solution: The unit of current is the **ampere** (symbol A), often shortened to "amp", named after André-Marie Ampère. Because it is named after a person, the full name is written with a small letter and the symbol with a capital: "2 amperes", "2 A".
